Slicing fields and point densities

Source: vignettes/articles/field-slices.Rmd
field-slices.Rmd

Inspect values inside a three-dimensional field by drawing sections through it. This article builds horizontal and oblique slices, adds contour lines and estimates density slices from point observations. It assumes the mappings in Get started; Preparing data for 3D layers explains coordinate keys, and Rendering volumes and traced surfaces shows views through a whole volume.

  1. Supply a complete coordinate grid and its values.

  2. Choose slice positions or an oblique plane.

  3. For point observations, choose a density bandwidth and inspect its effect.

Example 

library(ggplot2)
library(ggplot3d)

Supplying a scalar field

A scalar field assigns one value to each position. The table needs continuous x, y and z columns plus a numeric value column. This example samples a smooth concentration centred at the origin, with faster decay along y. Coordinates and values use arbitrary units.

axis <- seq(-1, 1, length.out = 11)
field <- expand.grid(x = axis, y = axis, z = axis)
field$value <- with(field, exp(-(x^2 + 2 * y^2 + z^2)))
stopifnot(nrow(field) == 11L^3L,
  !anyDuplicated(field[c("x", "y", "z")]))
range(field$value)
#> [1] 0.01831564 1.00000000

Map the scalar to value while z remains the vertical position. A horizontal slice at z = 0 shows the field’s central cross-section. Its default fill represents the mean interpolated value on each triangle. Slices are unlit by default, so their colours follow the fill scale directly.

p <- ggplot(field, aes(x, y, z = z, value = value))
colours <- scale_fill_gradient(low = "#DCEAF3", high = "#2E6F9E",
  limits = c(0, 1), breaks = c(0, 0.5, 1), labels = c("0", "0.5", "1"),
  name = "Value")
horizontal <- p + geom_slice_3d(zslice = 0) + colours +
  coord_3d(aspect = "data")
horizontal

The stat returns triangle corners with a slice label and a face value. Inspecting these columns shows which section was drawn and the range represented by its fill. Several corners belong to each face, so a row count measures geometry in this table.

section <- layer_data(horizontal)
unique(section$slice)
#> [1] z = 0
#> Levels: z = 0
range(section$value)
#> [1] 0.07447751 0.96130193

Choosing planes and contours

Pass several positions to draw parallel slices. Keeping the same fill limits lets their colours be compared directly. At z = -0.6 and z = 0.6 this symmetric field has matching values; the view reveals different parts of the two planes through their overlap.

p + geom_slice_3d(zslice = c(-0.6, 0.6)) + colours +
  coord_3d(aspect = "data")

The x and y slice arguments choose perpendicular sections. With all slice arguments omitted, the layer draws one central plane along each axis. Contour slices use the same positions; explicit breaks select the values traced by their lines.

p + geom_slice_3d(zslice = 0) +
  geom_slice_contour_3d(zslice = 0, breaks = c(0.3, 0.5, 0.7),
                        colour = "black", linewidth = 0.6) +
  colours + coord_3d(aspect = "data", elevation = 55)

An oblique plane uses a normal vector and a point on the plane. The normal below gives the plane x - y + z = 0 through the origin. The slice is sampled on a lattice and clipped to the field box; n sets the sampling resolution on this plane.

plane <- sdf_plane(c(1, -1, 1), point = c(0, 0, 0))
p + stat_slice_3d(slice = plane, n = 14) +
  stat_slice_contour_3d(slice = plane, n = 14,
    breaks = c(0.3, 0.5, 0.7), colour = "black", linewidth = 0.6) +
  colours + coord_3d(aspect = "data")

Slice positions use transformed coordinate units. For example, a z slice at 1 lies at an original height of 10 after a base-ten logarithmic transformation. Scaling heights and facet ranges explains those transformations. Axis-aligned slices use the input grid positions along their other axes; increasing n refines oblique sampling.

Preserving missing field values

Every coordinate combination must appear once. A missing measurement belongs in the value column as NA. Interpolation uses the surrounding grid corners, so missing values remove triangles that depend on them. This copy masks a small central column of the field while preserving all coordinate rows.

masked <- field
masked$value[abs(masked$x) < 0.21 & abs(masked$y) < 0.21] <- NA_real_
stopifnot(nrow(masked) == nrow(field))
ggplot(masked, aes(x, y, z = z, value = value)) +
  geom_slice_3d(zslice = 0) + colours +
  coord_3d(aspect = "data", elevation = 55)

A plane outside the grid has no field section to draw. Check the coordinate ranges when a requested slice is empty. Use Building surfaces and solids to extract a boundary at a chosen field value.

Estimating density from points

Point observations supply positions alone. The density-slice layer estimates a Gaussian product-kernel density on a grid, then sections that estimate. These simulated observations form two clouds separated along x, each with 40 points. A fixed seed reproduces the sample.

set.seed(17)
cloud <- data.frame(x = c(rnorm(40, -0.65, 0.18), rnorm(40, 0.65, 0.18)),
                    y = rnorm(80, 0, 0.25), z = rnorm(80, 0, 0.25))
stopifnot(nrow(cloud) == 80L)
summary(cloud)
#>        x                   y                   z           
#>  Min.   :-1.290105   Min.   :-0.549776   Min.   :-0.61369  
#>  1st Qu.:-0.631816   1st Qu.:-0.128130   1st Qu.:-0.24221  
#>  Median :-0.144341   Median : 0.007778   Median :-0.07926  
#>  Mean   : 0.003794   Mean   : 0.004676   Mean   :-0.02747  
#>  3rd Qu.: 0.666813   3rd Qu.: 0.181828   3rd Qu.: 0.15131  
#>  Max.   : 1.089619   Max.   : 0.729018   Max.   : 0.59830

The bandwidth controls smoothing in the units of each transformed axis. Choose three bandwidths when the axes need different smoothing. The scalar bandwidth here applies equally to all three axes, and the explicit limits leave room around the observations.

points <- ggplot(cloud, aes(x, y, z = z))
density_colours <- scale_fill_gradient(low = "#DCEAF3", high = "#2E6F9E",
  limits = c(0, 1.5), breaks = c(0, 0.75, 1.5), labels = c("0", "0.75", "1.5"),
  name = "Density")
density <- points + geom_density_slice_3d(zslice = 0, h = 0.25, n = 16) +
  geom_point_3d(size = 1, colour = "black") +
  density_colours +
  xlim(-1.5, 1.5) + ylim(-1, 1) + zlim(-1, 1) + coord_3d()
density

The computed density is density per three-dimensional volume, evaluated on the plane. It retains the smoothing contribution of observations away from that plane. It is suitable for locating concentrations through a cloud.

range(layer_data(density)$density)
#> [1] 0.001119723 0.762238628

Increasing the bandwidth spreads each observation’s contribution over a larger region. The next plot doubles the bandwidth and keeps the same coordinates and colour limits so the two estimates can be compared. Grid resolution controls sampling of that estimate; it is a separate choice from smoothing.

points + stat_density_slice_3d(zslice = 0, h = 0.5, n = 16) +
  geom_point_3d(size = 1, colour = "black") +
  density_colours +
  xlim(-1.5, 1.5) + ylim(-1, 1) + zlim(-1, 1) + coord_3d()

For nested density boundaries around the observations, use the probability-content examples in Building surfaces and solids. For selected planes through supplied measurements, use the scalar-field slices above. Combining 2D and 3D graphics places separate two-dimensional plots on parallel planes.
